nodes.title: Affinity diagram
nodes.summary: Article on the affinity diagram, a tool for organising ideas and data into groups by natural relationship. It attributes the term to Jiro Kawakita in the 1960s (also called the KJ method) and lists it among the seven management and planning tools.

nodes.title: Anchoring effect
nodes.summary: The anchoring effect is the tendency for a first number or piece of information to pull later judgments towards it, even when people know the anchor is arbitrary. The article covers the experiments behind the idea, proposed explanations, and where anchoring shows up, including negotiation and pricing.

nodes.title: Bookkeeping
nodes.summary: Explains bookkeeping: recording a business's financial transactions day to day so that accurate financial reports can be produced. It covers single-entry and double-entry systems, daybooks and ledgers, and the line between bookkeeping and accounting.

nodes.title: Card sorting
nodes.summary: Article on card sorting, a technique where participants sort items into groups to show how they categorise a domain. It is used in UX design and information architecture, with open (participants name the groups) and closed (groups given) variants.

nodes.title: Case study
nodes.summary: The article defines a case study as an in-depth examination of one case in its real-world context, used across medicine, business, politics and other fields. It covers how cases are selected, how case studies are designed and the long-running debate about how far findings from one case generalise.

nodes.title: Cash flow
nodes.summary: Introduces cash flow: payments made into or out of a business, project or financial product, usually discussed as expected future flows that have to be forecast. It covers how cash flow differs from profit and how cash flow statements are used.

nodes.title: Community of practice
nodes.summary: Article on communities of practice: groups who share a concern for something they do and learn to do it better by interacting regularly. It credits Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger (1991) and Wenger's later book, and describes the domain, community and practice that define one.

nodes.title: Contextual inquiry
nodes.summary: Article on contextual inquiry, a research method from contextual design: a roughly two-hour one-to-one session where the researcher watches someone do their normal work and discusses it with them as it happens.

nodes.title: Coworking
nodes.summary: Article on coworking: self-employed people and workers from different companies sharing an office, with shared infrastructure and services. It notes cost savings and convenience, and that coworking helps people avoid the isolation of working alone.

nodes.title: Customer experience
nodes.summary: Article on customer experience (CX): a customer's cognitive, emotional, sensory and behavioral responses across all stages of interacting with a product or service, before, during and after purchase. It covers measurement, touchpoints and journey mapping. I searched for "customer journey" and was redirected here.

nodes.title: Dark mode
nodes.summary: Covers dark mode, also called a dark theme or light-on-dark color scheme: interfaces that show light text and elements on a dark background, now offered as an option by many websites and operating systems. The article discusses its history, claimed benefits such as less eye strain and lower power use on OLED screens…

nodes.title: Decoy effect
nodes.summary: The decoy effect is when adding a third, clearly worse option changes which of two other options people prefer. The decoy is "asymmetrically dominated": worse than one option on every attribute, but only partly worse than the other, so it makes the dominating option look better.

nodes.title: Design system
nodes.summary: Describes a design system: a framework of standards, reusable components and documentation that keeps an organisation's digital products consistent and acts as a single source of truth for designers and developers. Parts can include component libraries, style guides, design languages, coded components and documentat…

nodes.title: Diary studies
nodes.summary: Article on diary studies: participants log entries about an activity over a period of time, giving longitudinal, in-context data at lower cost than field research. It notes the method is also called experience sampling, and discusses formats (paper, online, app) and trade-offs such as participant fatigue and less de…

nodes.title: Down payment
nodes.summary: Defines a down payment: an initial partial payment made up front when buying expensive goods or services, usually at the time the deal is finalised, with the remainder paid later, often through a loan.

nodes.title: Fixed-price contract
nodes.summary: A fixed-price contract sets a payment that is not adjusted for the resources, costs or time the contractor actually uses. The article contrasts it with cost-plus, time-and-materials and labor-hour contracts, and notes that it puts the cost risk on the contractor.

nodes.title: Freelancer
nodes.summary: The article covers freelancers as self-employed people not committed long-term to one employer: common fields, how freelancers find work (directly, through agencies or online platforms), the trade-offs in income stability and benefits, and the growth of platform-based freelancing.

nodes.title: Generative AI
nodes.summary: Article on generative AI: models that learn patterns from training data and generate new text, images, video, audio or code, usually from natural language prompts. It covers history, model types, applications, and concerns including accuracy, bias, copyright and labour.

nodes.title: Green computing
nodes.summary: Article on green computing (green IT), the study and practice of environmentally sustainable computing: energy use of devices and data centers, hardware lifecycle, recycling and efficient software.

nodes.title: Heuristic evaluation
nodes.summary: Article on heuristic evaluation, a usability inspection method in which evaluators judge an interface against recognised usability principles. It describes common heuristic sets and the method's appeal when budgets do not allow user testing.

nodes.title: Impostor syndrome
nodes.summary: Impostor syndrome, or the impostor phenomenon, is the experience of feeling like an intellectual or professional fraud despite evidence of competence. The article covers its original description in the 1970s, who reports it, the overlap with perfectionism and anxiety, and the debate about whether it is a syndrome at…

nodes.title: Inclusive design
nodes.summary: Article on inclusive design: designing products, services and environments usable by as many people as possible, especially groups traditionally excluded. It positions accessibility as one outcome of inclusive design, with a focus on meeting many different needs rather than an average user.

nodes.title: Invoice
nodes.summary: The encyclopedia article on invoices: the commercial document a seller issues to a buyer, listing what was supplied, the agreed prices and the terms of sale, including when payment is due.

nodes.title: Late fee
nodes.summary: Describes late fees: charges for paying a bill, or returning a rented or borrowed item, after its due date. They are most often associated with creditors, rental businesses and libraries, and are usually calculated per day or per item.

nodes.title: Likert scale
nodes.summary: Article on the Likert scale, the psychometric scale named after Rensis Likert and the most widely used way of scaling answers in survey research. It covers item format, the difference between a Likert item and a scale, and arguments about treating the answers as interval data.

nodes.title: Online banking
nodes.summary: Encyclopedia overview of online banking (also called internet, digital or web banking): customers of a bank or other financial institution view account information and carry out transactions through the institution's website or app. The article notes it has been the most common way customers reach their accounts sin…

nodes.title: Online public access catalog
nodes.summary: Encyclopedia article on the online public access catalog (OPAC), now usually just called the library catalog: an online database of what a library or group of libraries holds, which has largely replaced card catalogs.

nodes.title: Peer learning
nodes.summary: Article on peer learning: learners interacting with other learners to reach educational goals, moving from independent to interdependent learning. It compares it with cooperative learning and notes broader views outside formal education.

nodes.title: Professional liability insurance
nodes.summary: Explains professional liability insurance (also called professional indemnity, or errors and omissions): cover for the cost of defending and settling claims that a professional's advice or service was negligent or caused a client financial loss. It is distinct from general liability cover and is sometimes required b…

nodes.title: Public speaking
nodes.summary: Public speaking is delivering a speech to a live audience to inform, teach or persuade. The article covers its history from classical rhetoric, the main purposes of a speech, training and practice, the use of visual aids such as slides, and fear of public speaking.

nodes.title: Referral marketing
nodes.summary: Referral marketing is a structured version of word of mouth: a company actively encourages, and often rewards, existing customers for introducing new ones, so that referrals can be tracked and measured rather than left to chance.

nodes.title: Request for proposal
nodes.summary: A request for proposal (RFP) is a procurement document in which an organization asks potential suppliers for business proposals, usually as part of a structured bidding process. The article describes it as a form of reverse auction and covers typical contents, scoring and the related request for information and requ…

nodes.title: Revenue sharing
nodes.summary: Defines revenue sharing: dividing the income from sales among the people who contributed to them. It differs from profit sharing, which divides what is left after costs, and from holding shares in a company.

nodes.title: Screen reader
nodes.summary: Encyclopedia article on screen readers: assistive technology that renders text and images as speech or braille, essential for blind people and useful for people with low vision, learning disabilities or other print disabilities. The lead explains that they convey what is on screen through text-to-speech, sound cues …

nodes.title: Semi-structured interview
nodes.summary: Article on the semi-structured interview: an interviewer works from a framework of themes rather than a fixed list of questions, leaving room for new ideas from the interviewee.

nodes.title: Service blueprint
nodes.summary: Article on the service blueprint, a process chart of service delivery that shows customer actions alongside internal operations. It describes the usual lanes (customer actions, onstage and backstage staff actions, support processes) and the line of visibility between what customers see and what they do not.

nodes.title: Service design
nodes.summary: Article on service design: planning and arranging the people, infrastructure, communication and material parts of a service to improve its quality and the interaction between provider and user. It covers history, methods (journey maps, blueprints, prototyping services) and its relation to design thinking and managem…

nodes.title: Software license
nodes.summary: The article on software licenses: legal instruments that govern how software may be used or redistributed, from proprietary end-user licenses to free and open-source ones, and the difference between owning a copy and holding a license to use it.

nodes.title: Sole proprietorship
nodes.summary: Defines a sole proprietorship: a business owned and run by one person, with no legal distinction between the owner and the business. The owner keeps all profit and carries all liabilities personally. A sole trader may still employ people.

nodes.title: Statement of work
nodes.summary: Short project management article: a statement of work is a narrative description of the work a vendor will do for a client, with activities, deliverables and timelines, often with requirements, pricing and standard terms. It usually accompanies a master service agreement or follows a request for proposal.

nodes.title: System usability scale
nodes.summary: Short article on the SUS: a ten-item Likert-style questionnaire giving an overall view of how usable people find a system. It credits John Brooke at Digital Equipment Corporation, 1986, where it was made for office systems, and explains the alternating positive and negative items and the conversion to a 0 to 100 score.

nodes.title: Thematic analysis
nodes.summary: Article on thematic analysis, a common way to identify, analyse and interpret patterns of meaning in qualitative data. It describes it as an umbrella for several approaches, contrasted with fuller methodologies such as grounded theory.

nodes.title: Think aloud protocol
nodes.summary: Article on the think-aloud protocol as a data-gathering method in usability testing, psychology and the social sciences. It distinguishes concurrent thinking aloud (during the task) from retrospective (after it) and notes that verbalising can change how people do the task.

nodes.title: Usability testing
nodes.summary: Overview of usability testing: evaluating a product by watching representative users try real tasks, as distinct from inspection methods where experts judge the interface. It covers what tests measure (efficiency, accuracy, recall, emotional response), common setups including remote and hallway testing, and the long…

nodes.title: User-centered design
nodes.summary: Article on user-centered design: a framework in which usability goals, user characteristics, environment, tasks and workflow get attention at every stage of design, with testing throughout.

nodes.title: Value-based pricing
nodes.summary: The article describes value-based pricing as setting a price from the value a buyer perceives in a good or service, often framed as willingness to pay, rather than from what it costs to produce. Its example is a painting priced far above the cost of canvas and paint because of what owning it means to the buyer.

nodes.title: Web accessibility
nodes.summary: Article on web accessibility: making sure websites have no barriers for people with disabilities. It covers kinds of disability and assistive technology, the curb cut effect (benefits to people with situational limits or slow connections), WCAG, and laws in various countries.

nodes.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
